screens.title: Deploying to Public Testnets
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to move smart contracts beyond a local node and test them on a public Ethereum testnet. Public testnets provide the exact protocol behavior of mainnet but use test Ether, so you can exercise deployments, user flows, and verification without financial risk. You’ll see why Sepolia has become the primary choice, how to configure your Hardhat project to talk to a remote RPC provider, how to safely store A P I keys and private keys using environment variables, how to get test Ether from faucets, and how to verify a deployed contract on a block explorer. A concrete example in this chapter walks through deploying a simple Counter contract to Sepolia, showing the exact Hardhat commands and the deploy script output. We also cover the common mistakes developers encounter — like out of gas errors, incorrect RPC URLs, and accidentally committing secrets — and how to fix them. By the end you’ll know how to run a real deployment, confirm the transaction on a block explorer, and why testnets are the essential step between local development and mainnet launch. Think about the last time a local test missed a network-specific bug: this chapter helps you catch those before they become costly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives guide what you will practice and verify in this chapter. First, you will understand why public testnets exist and how they differ from local chains. That conceptual understanding helps you choose when to move from local testing to a public network. Second, you will configure your Hardhat or Truffle project to target a specific testnet like Sepolia. This includes adding the RPC URL, the chain identifier, and the wallet account configuration. Third, you will acquire test Ether from faucets and learn to manage A P I keys for RPC providers such as Alchemy or Infura. These skills let you fund deployments and maintain stable RPC access. Fourth, you will execute a real deployment and verify the resulting transaction on a block explorer. Verification completes the deployment loop and gives you a persistent address you can share or use in frontends. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone you can test: deploy a simple Counter contract to Sepolia, confirm the transaction on Sepolia Etherscan, and show you used environment variables for secrets. Throughout, we emphasize secure key handling and common deployment errors so you can deploy confidently and safely.

screens.title: What is a Public Testnet and Why Use Sepolia
screens.narratorSegment: A public testnet is a fully public blockchain that mirrors mainnet protocol rules but uses valueless test Ether so teams can test deployments and real user flows without financial risk. Testnets run the same transaction and consensus mechanics, so a contract that compiles and behaves locally might still fail on a public network because of gas rules, RPC behavior, or tooling differences. Sepolia is highlighted in this chapter as the primary testnet to use; it replaces older choices in many workflows and is supported by common RPC providers. Consider a concrete example: you have a frontend that interacts with a deployed contract; on a local network the provider responds instantly and mining is immediate, but on Sepolia you see real propagation delays, pending transactions, and real miner-driven gas dynamics. Testing on Sepolia surfaces UI and timing bugs, gas estimation issues, and verification differences that local testing can miss. A common misconception is that passing local tests guarantees mainnet readiness. That is false: local networks often bypass node-side constraints. Your takeaway is simple: use testnets to validate real network behavior and to practice the full deployment and verification workflow before risking mainnet funds. How will you adapt your testing schedule now that you can reproduce mainnet conditions safely?

content.html:
Definition › What is a Public Testnet
Definition and value

A public testnet runs the same protocol rules as mainnet but uses test Ether. It exposes network timing, gas, and node behaviors you cannot see locally.

Concrete example
Deploy a contract and interact from a frontend to observe pending transactions and gas estimation differences.
Common misconception
Passing local tests does not guarantee mainnet success; local nodes often shortcut mining and timing.
Why Sepolia
Preferred public testnet

Sepolia is the recommended public testnet in this chapter. It is supported by RPC providers and block explorers used for verification.

Analogy
Think of Sepolia as a rehearsal stage where the lights, sound, and timing are the same as the theater you’ll perform in.
Key Takeaway
Always include a public testnet step in your release checklist to catch network-specific failures.

screens.title: Configuring Hardhat for Sepolia
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Hardhat to deploy to Sepolia requires three practical pieces: an RPC URL from a provider, a wallet private key for signing transactions, and the network chainId. The RPC URL is the endpoint your tools use to speak to remote nodes; you usually get this after registering with an RPC provider. The private key funds the deployment and signs transactions, and you must never hardcode it into source control. Instead, create a. env file in your project root and add entries like SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY, then load them with the dotenv package from your Hardhat config. A concrete configuration sets the sepolia network with url: process. env. SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and accounts: PRIVATE_KEY!== undefined? [process. env. PRIVATE_KEY] : []. Also include chainId: 11155111 for Sepolia. A common error is forgetting to add. env to. gitignore or committing the file; that exposes your private key if your repo is public. Another mistake is using the wrong RPC endpoint or an expired A P I key, which causes connection failures. After configuring, test the connection by running a simple script that fetches the deployer address and balance. This validates secrets loading and RPC connectivity before you attempt deployment.

keyIdea.title: Secure config
keyIdea.text: Use environment variables for SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY and set chainId to Sepolia's identifier in your config file.

content.html:
Process › Configuring Hardhat
Checklist
  • Get an RPC URL from an RPC provider and store it as SEPOLIA_RPC_URL.
  • Place your wallet PRIVATE_KEY into a .env file and add .env to .gitignore.
  • Set chainId to Sepolia's numeric id when defining the network.
Common mistake
Hardcoding private keys or committing .env to source control.
Key Takeaway

Always use environment variables for secrets and confirm connectivity with a quick balance check before deploying.

Example Hardhat snippet
// hardhat.config.js snippet
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");
require("dotenv").config();

const SEPOLIA_RPC_URL = process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL;
const PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;

module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.20",
  networks: {
    sepolia: {
      url: SEPOLIA_RPC_URL,
      accounts: PRIVATE_KEY ? [PRIVATE_KEY] : [],
      chainId: 11155111
    }
  }
};
Run a quick script that prints the deployer address and balance to verify the RPC and secrets are loaded.

screens.title: Hardhat Config Example Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided hardhat. config. js example and explain each section. First, the toolbox plugin imports common tasks and helpers for compilation and verification. The dotenv call ensures environment variables in. env are loaded at runtime; this is where your SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY come from. We assign these to constants so the network block can reference them. In networks. sepolia we provide url, accounts, and chainId. The url tells Hardhat which node to contact, accounts supplies the signer for transactions — using an array of one private key — and chainId ensures the network is identified correctly. The etherscan apiKey entry is used later for contract verification on Sepolia Etherscan. A potential pitfall here is leaving PRIVATE_KEY undefined or incorrectly formatted; if PRIVATE_KEY is missing the accounts array will be empty and deployment will fail with an authorization or insufficient funds error. Another subtle issue is pasting the RPC URL from the provider that targets the wrong network; the chain will not accept transactions if chainId and the RPC target do not match. After reviewing the config, save it and run a compile and a small script that uses getSigners to check that your deployer account resolves correctly. That quick check catches misconfigurations early.

keyIdea.title: Config walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Each config field maps to a runtime need: RPC URL for node access, accounts for signing, chainId for network identity, and etherscan apiKey for verification.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › hardhat.config.js
Why dotenv?
Loading secrets at runtime prevents accidental exposure in source control. It keeps API keys and private keys out of your committed files.
Accounts behavior
If PRIVATE_KEY is undefined the accounts array is empty and Hardhat cannot sign deployments. Always verify the environment variable before deploying.
Pro tip: test your config by calling getSigners and printing the balance.
Snippet
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");
require("dotenv").config();

const SEPOLIA_RPC_URL = process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL;
const PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;

module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.20",
  networks: {
    sepolia: {
      url: SEPOLIA_RPC_URL,
      accounts: PRIVATE_KEY ? [PRIVATE_KEY] : [],
      chainId: 11155111
    }
  },
  etherscan: { apiKey: process.env.ETHERSCAN_API_KEY }
};
Check: correct RPC, presence of PRIVATE_KEY, and etherscan API key before deploying.

screens.title: Deploy Script Explained
screens.narratorSegment: The deploy script provided demonstrates a minimal pattern for deploying a contract with Hardhat. It starts by getting the signer or deployer account using getSigners; that reveals which account will fund the deployment. Next it gets the contract factory for the compiled contract and calls deploy with any constructor arguments. The script awaits waitForDeployment to ensure the transaction is mined and the contract is present on the network. After that, it prints the deployed contract address so you can copy it for verification or frontend wiring. A concrete example in this chapter deploys a MyContract with a constructor string argument. A common misconception is expecting the deployment to be instantaneous as in local networks; on Sepolia you should wait for mining and confirm by checking the transaction hash on a block explorer. Another pitfall is failing to compile before running the deploy script; running npx hardhat compile first ensures contract artifacts are present. Finally, wrap the deployment call in a try/catch to surface errors such as insufficient funds or RPC connectivity problems. This pattern keeps your deployment predictable and debuggable.

keyIdea.title: Deploy flow
keyIdea.text: Use getSigners, getContractFactory, deploy, and waitForDeployment to ensure contracts are mined and you have a valid address.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › scripts/deploy.js
Deploy script
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();
  console.log("Deploying with account:", deployer.address);

  const MyContract = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyContract");
  const myContract = await MyContract.deploy("Hello, Sepolia!");

  await myContract.waitForDeployment();

  console.log("MyContract deployed to:", myContract.target);
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
Concrete example
Deploy a Counter contract, then paste the printed address into Sepolia Etherscan to view the transaction.
Misconception
Deployments are not instantaneous on public testnets; wait for mining and check the explorer for confirmation.
Key Takeaway

Use waitForDeployment and inspect the explorer to ensure your contract is live before interacting further.

screens.title: Getting Test Ether from Faucets
screens.narratorSegment: Before any public deployment you must fund your deployment wallet with test Ether. Faucets are the services that distribute small amounts of testnet Ether for free. The process typically asks for your wallet address and sometimes a CAPTCHA, and some faucets may require a short social proof action. For Sepolia, use the faucet endpoints recommended by your RPC provider or the official community faucets that target Sepolia. Be aware that faucets can be rate-limited or temporarily out of funds, so plan ahead and request test Ether well before your deployment window. A concrete example: copy the address derived from your PRIVATE_KEY into the faucet form, request the allocation, then check the balance with a quick RPC call or by viewing the address on Sepolia Etherscan. If the faucet appears empty, try alternate faucets or wait for replenishment. A common mistake is sending test Ether to the wrong network address or using a faucet for a different testnet. Always double-check that the faucet dispenses Sepolia test Ether and that your config points to Sepolia. Once funded, confirm the balance before starting the deployment to avoid out-of-gas errors.

keyIdea.title: Faucet planning
keyIdea.text: Request Sepolia test Ether in advance, verify the correct network, and confirm your wallet balance before deploying.

content.html:
Process › Getting Test Ether
Step-by-step
  1. Derive your wallet address from the PRIVATE_KEY and copy it.
  2. Visit a Sepolia faucet and paste the address, complete any required checks, and request funds.
  3. Wait for the faucet transaction and verify the balance via RPC or Sepolia Etherscan.
Pitfall
Using a faucet for a different testnet will leave your Sepolia wallet unfunded; double-check the network name.
Check
After requesting test Ether, confirm the balance with an RPC balance call or by entering the address into Sepolia Etherscan.
Practical note
If a faucet is rate-limited, schedule your request earlier or use multiple faucets to aggregate enough test Ether for your deployment gas costs.
Key Takeaway

Fund your deployer in advance and verify balance to avoid deployment interruptions caused by out-of-gas errors.

screens.title: Local Network vs Public Testnet
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between a local network and a public testnet is essential for correct expectations during deployment. Local networks like Hardhat Network or Ganache are designed for fast iteration: they mine instantly, run in-memory, and often bypass network propagation delays. This makes them perfect for unit tests and quick debugging. Public testnets like Sepolia, however, behave like mainnet: transactions take time to propagate, miners include transactions in blocks, gas estimation matters, and RPC providers may throttle requests. A concrete contrast: a contract deployment on a local node is immediate and returns an address quickly, but on Sepolia you’ll submit a transaction, watch it go from pending to mined, and then confirm it on Sepolia Etherscan. Misconceptions arise when developers assume local success means mainnet readiness. That assumption overlooks real network variables such as RPC rate limits, gas spikes, or verification nuances. The practical takeaway is to use both: run unit tests locally, then run integration tests on Sepolia to verify realistic behavior. Which part of your workflow will you move to Sepolia integration testing next? Local Network vs Public Testnet means local networks are fast and permissive; public testnets mirror real network constraints and timing.. In practical terms, key differences to understand before you deploy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Local networks are fast and permissive; public testnets mirror real network constraints and timing.

content.html:
Comparison › Local vs Public Testnet
Local Network (Hardhat/Ganache)
  • Instant mining and execution for rapid iteration.
  • No network propagation or real RPC rate limits.
  • Great for unit testing and debugging logic.
Misconception
Passing local tests does not guarantee network readiness.
Public Testnet (Sepolia)
  • Real mining delays, gas dynamics, and node behaviors.
  • Requires test Ether from faucets and proper RPC configuration.
  • Necessary for integration tests and verification workflows.
Key Takeaway
Use both: local for fast iteration, Sepolia to validate real network conditions.

screens.title: RPC Providers and API Keys
screens.narratorSegment: RPC providers like Alchemy or Infura run and expose Ethereum nodes you can use via an RPC URL and an A P I key. When you sign up, the provider gives you a dedicated RPC endpoint for a chosen network and an A P I key to authenticate and meter your requests. Using a provider improves reliability and reduces the chance of running into a flaky node. In practice, you place the provider URL into SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and include the provider-issued A P I key inside that URL or as part of the provider dashboard settings. A concrete example: your Hardhat config will include the provider URL so compilation, deployment, and verification commands route through that provider. Another common issue is using an expired or rotated A P I key inadvertently, which results in authentication failures. The recommended approach is to monitor usage on the provider dashboard and keep A P I keys in environment variables so they can be rotated safely without code changes. Treat the RPC provider as a critical infrastructure piece for stable deployments.

Providers host nodes so you do not need to run your own. They supply endpoints and API keys that your dev tools call for compilation, queries, and transactions.

Stability, scaling, and provider dashboards for monitoring.
Caveats

Practical

screens.title: Running the Deployment Command
screens.narratorSegment: When you run the Hardhat deployment command targeting Sepolia, several steps happen sequentially. First, Hardhat compiles contracts if needed, producing artifacts for the contract factory. Next, Hardhat connects to the RPC endpoint defined in your config using the SEPOLIA_RPC_URL, authenticating with any provider A P I key embedded in that URL. The deployer account is derived from the PRIVATE_KEY and used to sign the deployment transaction. Hardhat then broadcasts the signed transaction to the network. On a public testnet this transaction enters a pending state and must be mined into a block. You should watch the console output for the transaction hash and then confirm that transaction on Sepolia Etherscan. If the transaction runs out of gas, the network will reject it and you’ll see an error; to fix that increase gasLimit or ensure the wallet has sufficient test Ether. Another important point is timing: unlike local networks, mining on Sepolia takes real time, so allow several confirmations before interacting with the contract. This process builds a mental model of how your tooling, provider, and the network work together during a real deployment.

keyIdea.text: Compile, connect via RPC, sign with private key, broadcast, and wait for mining — verify the transaction on Sepolia Etherscan.

Process Flow › Deployment Command
Command
npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.js --network sepolia
Lifecycle
  1. Compile contracts into artifacts.
  2. Connect to RPC using SEPOLIA_RPC_URL.
  3. Sign transaction with PRIVATE_KEY and broadcast.
  4. Wait for mining, then log the deployed address.
Console outputs to watch
  • Deployer address and balance
  • Transaction hash for the deployment
  • Final deployed contract address
Troubleshooting
Out-of-gas or connection errors indicate a need to increase gasLimit or check your RPC/API key and balance.

Observe the transaction hash and confirm it on the explorer; on Sepolia, patience is part of the workflow.

screens.title: Verifying Contracts on Sepolia Etherscan
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the step where you publish your contract source code and metadata so block explorers can match it with the deployed bytecode. Verifying on Sepolia Etherscan provides transparency and allows others to read your contract code, view constructor arguments, and inspect the transaction. The etherscan apiKey in your Hardhat config enables automated verification tools. A typical workflow is to take the deployed contract address printed by your deploy script and run a verification command such as npx hardhat verify with the network flag and the contract address. This tool uses the A P I key to submit the source code and compilation settings to the explorer for matching and publication. A common error is attempting verification with incorrect constructor arguments or with the wrong compiler settings; both prevent a match and cause verification to fail. Another gotcha is verifying too soon; wait for the deployment transaction to be indexed by the explorer. The value of verification is both practical — making your address usable by frontends — and professional: it signals that you can reproduce and explain the code behind the contract. Try verifying a simple Counter contract after deployment to see the process end-to-end.

keyIdea.title: Why verify
keyIdea.text: Verification publishes source code and compilation metadata so explorers can match deployed bytecode and display human-readable contracts.

content.html:
Definition › Contract Verification
What verification does
It uploads your source code and compiler settings to the block explorer, which then attempts to match the deployed bytecode to your sources and publish a human-readable contract page.
Example command
npx hardhat verify --network sepolia  "ConstructorArg1"
Include the constructor arguments and ensure the compiler version and optimization settings match those used for deployment.
Troubleshooting
If verification fails, check the constructor arguments, compiler version, and optimization flags you used during compilation.
Key Takeaway

Verification completes the deployment cycle and makes your contract discoverable and auditable on Sepolia Etherscan.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Deployments to public testnets introduce a set of predictable pitfalls that you should plan for. The most common is an out-of-gas error: the deployment transaction did not include enough gas or the wallet lacked sufficient test Ether. The fix is to check your wallet balance, increase the gasLimit for the deployment if necessary, and request more test Ether from a faucet. Another frequent issue is an incorrect or expired RPC URL or A P I key — this shows up as connection or authentication errors. Confirm the SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and the provider dashboard to ensure the key is active. A different class of error is committing private keys to source control; if that happens, consider the private key compromised and rotate it. Also, verification failures often stem from mismatched constructor arguments or compiler settings; re-check your compiler version and optimization flags. Finally, impatience is a mistake: public testnets take real time to confirm transactions, so give the network time to mine and be indexed by the explorer. A small troubleshooting checklist — check balance, check RPC, check gasLimit, and wait — resolves most issues quickly.

content.html:
Core Concept › Troubleshooting
Out of Gas
Increase gasLimit or add test Ether from a faucet and retry.

Confirm the provider URL, that the API key is active, and that it targets Sepolia.

Re-check constructor args, compiler version, and optimization flags used during deployment.
Practical debugging checklist
  1. Check deployer balance on Sepolia.
  2. Confirm SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and provider key are correct.
  3. Increase gasLimit if needed and retry the transaction.
  4. Wait for mining and check Sepolia Etherscan for indexing delays.

In this chapter you will learn how to move smart contracts beyond a local node and test them on a public Ethereum testnet. Public testnets provide the exact protocol behavior of mainnet but use test Ether, so you can exercise deployments, user flows, and verification without financial risk. You’ll see why Sepolia has become the primary choice, how to configure your Hardhat project to talk to a remote RPC provider, how to safely store A P I keys and private keys using environment variables, how to get test Ether from faucets, and how to verify a deployed contract on a block explorer. A concrete example in this chapter walks through deploying a simple Counter contract to Sepolia, showing the exact Hardhat commands and the deploy script output. We also cover the common mistakes developers encounter — like out of gas errors, incorrect RPC URLs, and accidentally committing secrets — and how to fix them. By the end you’ll know how to run a real deployment, confirm the transaction on a block explorer, and why testnets are the essential step between local development and mainnet launch. Think about the last time a local test missed a network-specific bug: this chapter helps you catch those before they become costly.

These learning objectives guide what you will practice and verify in this chapter. First, you will understand why public testnets exist and how they differ from local chains. That conceptual understanding helps you choose when to move from local testing to a public network. Second, you will configure your Hardhat or Truffle project to target a specific testnet like Sepolia. This includes adding the RPC URL, the chain identifier, and the wallet account configuration. Third, you will acquire test Ether from faucets and learn to manage A P I keys for RPC providers such as Alchemy or Infura. These skills let you fund deployments and maintain stable RPC access. Fourth, you will execute a real deployment and verify the resulting transaction on a block explorer. Verification completes the deployment loop and gives you a persistent address you can share or use in frontends. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone you can test: deploy a simple Counter contract to Sepolia, confirm the transaction on Sepolia Etherscan, and show you used environment variables for secrets. Throughout, we emphasize secure key handling and common deployment errors so you can deploy confidently and safely.

On this practical objectives page we emphasize the hands-on skills you should demonstrate. You will reliably configure a project for Sepolia by adding a valid RPC URL and the correct chainId, and by wiring the wallet account through an environment variable. As a practical test, you should be able to create a. env file, ensure it is in. gitignore, and load it using the dotenv package. You'll demonstrate obtaining test Ether from a faucet and confirm the wallet balance before attempting a deployment. Then you will run a deploy script, observe the compile and broadcast steps, and retrieve the resulting contract address. Finally, you will perform verification on Sepolia Etherscan to ensure your published bytecode and ABI match the deployed contract. These objectives are intentionally operational: they focus on the concrete steps that prevent mistakes, such as misconfigured RPC URLs or committing a private key, and they prepare you to debug common errors. Finish by saving the contract address and confirming the transaction hash on the explorer.

A public testnet is a fully public blockchain that mirrors mainnet protocol rules but uses valueless test Ether so teams can test deployments and real user flows without financial risk. Testnets run the same transaction and consensus mechanics, so a contract that compiles and behaves locally might still fail on a public network because of gas rules, RPC behavior, or tooling differences. Sepolia is highlighted in this chapter as the primary testnet to use; it replaces older choices in many workflows and is supported by common RPC providers. Consider a concrete example: you have a frontend that interacts with a deployed contract; on a local network the provider responds instantly and mining is immediate, but on Sepolia you see real propagation delays, pending transactions, and real miner-driven gas dynamics. Testing on Sepolia surfaces UI and timing bugs, gas estimation issues, and verification differences that local testing can miss. A common misconception is that passing local tests guarantees mainnet readiness. That is false: local networks often bypass node-side constraints. Your takeaway is simple: use testnets to validate real network behavior and to practice the full deployment and verification workflow before risking mainnet funds. How will you adapt your testing schedule now that you can reproduce mainnet conditions safely?

Configuring Hardhat to deploy to Sepolia requires three practical pieces: an RPC URL from a provider, a wallet private key for signing transactions, and the network chainId. The RPC URL is the endpoint your tools use to speak to remote nodes; you usually get this after registering with an RPC provider. The private key funds the deployment and signs transactions, and you must never hardcode it into source control. Instead, create a. env file in your project root and add entries like SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY, then load them with the dotenv package from your Hardhat config. A concrete configuration sets the sepolia network with url: process. env. SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and accounts: PRIVATE_KEY!== undefined? [process. env. PRIVATE_KEY] : []. Also include chainId: 11155111 for Sepolia. A common error is forgetting to add. env to. gitignore or committing the file; that exposes your private key if your repo is public. Another mistake is using the wrong RPC endpoint or an expired A P I key, which causes connection failures. After configuring, test the connection by running a simple script that fetches the deployer address and balance. This validates secrets loading and RPC connectivity before you attempt deployment.

Let's walk through the provided hardhat. config. js example and explain each section. First, the toolbox plugin imports common tasks and helpers for compilation and verification. The dotenv call ensures environment variables in. env are loaded at runtime; this is where your SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY come from. We assign these to constants so the network block can reference them. In networks. sepolia we provide url, accounts, and chainId.
